The great wave of European migrants to Argentina between about 1880 and 1914, which turned it into a nation of immigrants. Millions arrived, mostly from Italy and Spain. By 1914 about a third of the country's people had been born abroad, and in Buenos Aires about half.

Argentina wanted them. Its 1853 constitution promised to encourage European immigration, and the writer Juan Bautista Alberdi summed up the idea as "to govern is to populate". After the army's Conquest of the Desert seized the southern pampas from Indigenous peoples in the late 1870s, vast farmlands opened up. Railways and refrigerated ships let Argentina export wheat and beef to Europe, and the country became one of the richest in the world.

Many Italians came only for the harvest and went home each year; they were called golondrinas, "swallows". Russian Jews founded farming colonies, and Syrians and Lebanese set up as traders.

Migrants packed into the tenements of Buenos Aires. Out of that mix came the tango, the Italian lilt of Buenos Aires Spanish and a strong labour movement.
